1a.html:
Development is both a physical reality and a state of mind in which society has secured the means for a better life. The physical reality is material: food, shelter, health, jobs and income. The state of mind is how people see themselves: dignity, confidence, hope. The poor themselves describe both hunger and shame.

The three core values join the two

  1. Sustenance, the ability to meet basic needs (food, shelter, health, protection). Without it there is absolute underdevelopment: the physical side.
  2. Self-esteem, to be a person: worth and respect, not being a tool of others. Nations seen as "underdeveloped" seek development partly to gain esteem: the mental side.
  3. Freedom from servitude, to be able to choose: release from want, ignorance, misery and domination. Growth matters because it widens choice (Lewis); this needs material means and a free mind.

They match the three objectives: more life-sustaining goods, higher levels of living and wider economic and social choices.
pts: Explains the statement: development secures the material means of a better life (physical reality) and changes how people see themselves (state of mind)
Sustenance: ability to meet basic needs (food, shelter, health, protection), the physical side
Self-esteem: to be a person, worth and respect, not a tool of others, the mental side
Freedom from servitude: to be able to choose, free from want, ignorance and domination
Links the values to both sides, for example freedom needing both income and a free mind, or the voices of the poor
Relates them to the three objectives of development
1a.src: Ch 1 Economic development (Todaro), slides 4-5, 23, 36; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., p 13; Standard textbook treatment
1a.watch:
• The 13th edition of Todaro drops the core-values section, but the slides keep "sustenance", "self-esteem" and "freedom" among the concepts for review (slide 36). Use these three words exactly.
  • "Freedom" here is freedom from servitude (to nature, ignorance, other people, misery), not only political freedom.

2a.html:
Project evaluation is the broad assessment of a project's worth from every side (technical, market, financial, economic, social, environmental) and at every stage: appraisal before, monitoring during and review after.

Cost-benefit analysis (CBA) is one technique within it: it values all social costs and benefits in money (shadow prices, externalities added, transfers excluded), discounts them and decides by NPV, BCR or IRR.

Differences

  • Scope: evaluation covers all aspects; CBA only the monetised welfare test.
  • Viewpoint: evaluation can be private; CBA takes society's view.
  • Prices: financial evaluation uses market prices and counts taxes; CBA uses shadow prices.
  • Timing: CBA is mainly ex-ante; evaluation also covers monitoring and ex-post review (a rural road checked against its traffic targets).

Examples

  • A private garment factory is evaluated financially (profit NPV at market prices, technical and market feasibility); no CBA is needed.
  • The Padma Bridge needed a CBA: travel-time and vehicle-cost savings beyond toll revenue, against construction, resettlement and environmental costs.

So every CBA is a project evaluation, but not every evaluation is a CBA.
pts: Project evaluation: broad, multi-aspect assessment (technical, financial, economic, social, environmental) at all stages
CBA: a technique that values social costs and benefits in money, discounts them and applies NPV, BCR or IRR
At least two differences: scope, viewpoint (owner or society), prices (market or shadow, transfers, externalities), timing
An example of evaluation that is not CBA (financial appraisal of a firm, or an ex-post review)
An example of CBA with its social benefits and costs (Padma Bridge, rural road, flood control or similar)
Concludes that CBA is one part or tool of project evaluation
2a.src: Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 607-608; CBA exam note, pp 1-2, 13; Cost-benefit analysis handout, handout parts I and IX; Standard textbook treatment
2a.watch:
• The slides do not define "project evaluation" separately; Todaro calls the microeconomic appraisal of public projects project appraisal and says it rests on social CBA. Any reading that treats CBA as the narrower, social, monetised test is sound.
  • Financial analysis versus economic CBA (hum-cbanote p 2) is the sharpest contrast; use the toll-road or bypass example if Padma is unfamiliar.

2b.html:
Cost-benefit analysis (CBA) is a systematic method for judging whether the social benefits of a project or policy exceed its social costs, by converting both into money values at a common point in time: net social benefit = social benefits - social costs.

Main purpose. Resources are scarce, so every project must justify itself against the best alternative use of the same money (its opportunity cost). CBA tells the government whether a project should be undertaken and, among alternatives (a bridge, a hospital, an embankment), which gives society the greatest net benefit. Unlike financial analysis, it counts externalities and non-market effects (time saved, flood damage avoided, pollution) and excludes transfers such as taxes. For example, it asks whether Tk 10 billion for coastal flood protection returns more in discounted avoided damage, lives saved and protected crops than it costs, including displacement.

Procedure

  1. Define the project and its alternatives, including the without-project case.
  2. Identify all relevant costs and benefits: direct, indirect and intangible; count only incremental effects (with versus without), and ignore sunk costs and transfers.
  3. Set the time horizon (project life).
  4. Measure the physical costs and benefits year by year.
  5. Assign money values: market prices, shadow prices where markets are distorted, and willingness to pay or consumer surplus for non-market effects.
  6. Select the discount rate: social opportunity cost of capital or social time preference rate.
  7. Calculate present values: PV = FV/(1+r)^t.
  8. Compute the criteria: NPV > 0, BCR > 1, IRR > r.
  9. Test sensitivity and risk: for example costs +20%, benefits -20%, a higher r; find switching values; build scenarios.
  10. Decide: accept, reject or rank, using judgement on distribution and intangibles.
pts: Defines CBA: social benefits against social costs, valued in money at a common point in time
Purpose: allocate scarce resources (opportunity cost) to the project or alternative with the greatest net social benefit; accept, reject or rank
Purpose: captures externalities and non-market effects that financial analysis misses, with an example
Step: define the project and alternatives, including the without-project case
Step: identify direct, indirect and intangible costs and benefits; incremental only; exclude sunk costs and transfers
Steps: time horizon and physical measurement year by year
Step: monetise with market or shadow prices, or willingness to pay
Steps: choose the discount rate and calculate present values
Step: compute NPV, BCR and IRR with their rules
Step: sensitivity and risk analysis (cost overrun, benefit shortfall, discount rate, switching value)
Step: final decision, with judgement on distribution and intangibles
2b.src: Cost-benefit analysis handout, handout parts I-III, IX-XII and 14; CBA exam note, pp 1-3, 10-13; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 607-610
2b.watch:
• The handout's ten steps are the expected list; Todaro's three-step version (objectives, shadow prices and social discount rate, decision criterion) is a valid summary but loses detail.
  • "With versus without" is not "before versus after": an irrigation scheme that raises farm revenue from Tk 50 million to Tk 70 million has a benefit of Tk 20 million.
  • CBA informs the decision; it does not replace judgement on distribution and unpriced effects.

3a.html:
Kuznets ratio: the share of national income received by the richest 20% divided by the share of the poorest 40%.

Gini coefficient: the area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve divided by the total area under the diagonal, G = A/(A+B), from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality).

Typical size distribution (Table 5.1). 20 individuals, national income 100 units, ranked from 0.8 to 15.0 units. Grouped in quintiles of four, their income shares are 5, 9, 13, 22 and 51%; the decile shares are 1.8, 3.2, 3.9, 5.1, 5.8, 7.2, 9.0, 13.0, 22.5, 28.5%.

Kuznets ratio:

\frac{\text{top } 20\%}{\text{bottom } 40\%} = \frac{51}{5 + 9} = 3.64

Gini. Cumulative decile shares give the Lorenz curve: 1.8, 5.0, 8.9, 14.0, 19.8, 27.0, 36.0, 49.0, 71.5, 100% at 10, 20, ..., 100% of population. The area under it, by trapezoids of width 0.1:

\begin{aligned} B &= \sum_{k=1}^{10} 0.1 \times \frac{Y_{k-1} + Y_k}{2} = 0.283 \\ A &= 0.5 - 0.283 = 0.217 \\ G &= \frac{A}{A + B} = \frac{0.217}{0.5} = 0.43 \end{aligned}

Using all 20 incomes gives 0.44, the textbook value.

Answer: Kuznets ratio 3.64 and Gini about 0.44: a relatively unequal distribution (equal countries lie near 0.20 to 0.35).
pts: Defines the Kuznets ratio: income share of the top 20% over that of the bottom 40%
Defines the Gini as A/(A+B) from the Lorenz curve, 0 to 1
Sets out a typical size distribution: ranked incomes grouped into quintile (and decile) shares
Kuznets ratio 51/14 = 3.64 (or the correct value for the student's own distribution)
Cumulative shares plotted as a Lorenz curve against the diagonal (table or sketch)
Computes the Gini from the areas: about 0.43 to 0.44 (or the correct value for the student's own data)
Interprets: higher ratio or Gini means more inequality; 0.44 is relatively unequal
3a.src: Ch 5 Poverty and inequality, slides 8-12; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 263-268
3a.watch:
• The question says "a typical size distribution", so the textbook's Table 5.1 is the natural choice; any consistent made-up distribution earns full credit if the arithmetic is right.
  • The ratio is top 20% over bottom 40% (51/14), not top 20% over bottom 20% (51/5).
  • Fewer groups understate the Gini: quintiles give 0.42, deciles 0.43, individuals 0.44.

3b.html:
Absolute poverty is an obvious concern, but social welfare also falls with inequality among people above the poverty line: welfare is W = W(Y, I, P), rising with income per head Y and falling with inequality I and poverty P. There are three main reasons.

1. Extreme inequality causes economic inefficiency

  • Credit: at a given average income, higher inequality means fewer people qualify for loans. The near-poor lack collateral, so they cannot educate their children or start and expand businesses.
  • Saving: the middle class has the highest marginal saving rate. The rich in many poor countries spend on luxury imports, gold, jewellery and foreign travel, or move savings abroad (capital flight).
  • Assets: inequality skews spending toward higher education rather than quality primary schooling, and toward huge estates beside tiny plots, though family and medium farms are most efficient.
  • The result is lower average income and slower growth, which in turn breeds more inequality.

2. It undermines social stability and solidarity

  • Concentrated income gives the rich political power, used for rent seeking (lobbying, donations, bribery, cronyism) and to block efficient reform.
  • It can push the poor toward self-defeating populism, and goes with civil strife (El Salvador, Iran) and violent crime. Politics turns to dividing the pie rather than enlarging it.

3. It is unfair. Behind Rawls' "veil of ignorance", not knowing who they would be, most people choose less inequality than exists, because much of it reflects luck and birth rather than effort.

Conclusion. Reducing inequality above the poverty line serves efficiency, stability and justice, not only charity.
pts: Frames the issue: welfare depends on inequality as well as on income and poverty, W(Y, I, P)
Inefficiency through credit: fewer qualify for loans, no collateral, so less education and enterprise
Inefficiency through saving: middle class saves most; the rich buy luxury imports or send capital abroad
Inefficient asset allocation, for example higher over primary education, or unequal land holdings
Concludes that high inequality lowers average income and growth
Political power of the rich: rent seeking and blocked institutional reform
Social instability: populism, civil conflict or violent crime
Unfairness: Rawls' veil of ignorance; inequality from luck and birth
Overall conclusion
3b.src: Ch 5 Poverty and inequality, slides 4-5, 32-33; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 274-276, 279-280
3b.watch:
• The question is about inequality above the poverty line, so do not answer with the harms of absolute poverty.
  • The three headings (inefficiency, instability, unfairness) are the course's own; keep them so the keywords match.
  • Some inequality is accepted as an incentive for effort and skill; the concern is extreme inequality.

4i.html:
Absolute poverty is being unable, or barely able, to meet the subsistence essentials of food, clothing and shelter. It is measured against a fixed real poverty line that does not move with average income: USD 1.90 a day at 2011 PPP internationally, or a national line costed from a basic food basket plus essential non-food items. In Bangladesh (2022) 18.7% were below the upper line and 5.6% below the lower line. Measures: headcount ratio, poverty gap, FGT index.

Relative poverty is being poor compared with others in the same society. Its line moves with average living standards (for example a share of median income), or it is judged by the income share of the poorest 20 or 40%. Inequality measures (income shares, Lorenz curve, Gini) capture it.

Contrast. Shared growth can eliminate absolute poverty; relative poverty persists unless the distribution narrows.
pts: Absolute poverty: unable to meet basic needs (food, clothing, shelter)
Measured against a fixed real line: USD 1.90 a day at 2011 PPP (the slides' figure; USD 1.25, 2.15 or 3.00 also credited) or the national lines
Measures or data: headcount, poverty gap or FGT, or Bangladesh's 18.7% and 5.6% (2022)
Relative poverty: deprivation compared with others in the same society
Relative line moves with average income (share of the median, or bottom quintile share), measured by inequality measures
Contrast: absolute poverty can be ended by shared growth; relative poverty remains while inequality remains
4i.src: Ch 5 Poverty and inequality, slides 18-24, 32, 44; Ch 1 Economic development (Todaro), slides 7-9; Dimensions of economic development (v3), slide 65; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 269-270, 275; Standard textbook treatment
4i.watch:
• The question prints 23 1/3 marks for any three of four notes, so each note carries 7.78 marks.
  • The slides give no numerical relative-poverty line; 50% or 60% of median income is common in rich countries, so quote it as an example only.
  • The international line has been revised: USD 1.25 at 2005 PPP, USD 1.90 at 2011 PPP (the slides), USD 2.15 at 2017 PPP from 2022 and, as reported, USD 3.00 at 2021 PPP from 2025. Quote the slides' figure; any of these with its PPP year is right.

4ii.html:
Foster-Greer-Thorbecke (FGT) index

FGT measures absolute poverty from each poor person's shortfall below the poverty line Y_p:

P_\alpha = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{H}\left(\frac{Y_p - Y_i}{Y_p}\right)^{\alpha}, \qquad \alpha \ge 0

Here N is the population, H the number of poor and Y_i the income of poor person i. \alpha = 0 gives the headcount ratio H/N; \alpha = 1 the normalised poverty gap (depth); \alpha = 2 the squared gap (severity), which weights the poorest most. Example: incomes 0.6, 0.6, 0.8, 0.8, 2, 2, 6, 6 with Y_p = 1 give P_0 = 0.5, P_1 = 0.15, P_2 = 0.05.

Purchasing power parity (PPP)

A PPP rate is the exchange rate that equalises the cost of the same basket in two countries (law of one price). A basket costing USD 1,800 in New York and HKD 10,800 in Hong Kong gives 6 HKD per USD. Non-traded goods are cheaper in poor countries, so PPP incomes (used in the HDI) compare living standards better: India's 2017 income per head was USD 1,820 at market rates, USD 7,060 at PPP.
pts: FGT formula P_\alpha = \frac{1}{N}\sum ((Y_p - Y_i)/Y_p)^\alpha over the poor, with the symbols defined
\alpha = 0 headcount ratio, \alpha = 1 poverty gap, \alpha = 2 squared gap (severity)
P_2 weights the poorest most (distribution-sensitive), or a worked example such as P_0 = 0.5, P_1 = 0.15, P_2 = 0.05
PPP: the exchange rate that equalises the cost of a common basket (law of one price)
A PPP example, for example 10,800 / 1,800 = 6 HKD per USD
Why PPP: non-traded goods are cheaper in poor countries, so PPP raises their measured income (for example India about four times); used in GNI and HDI comparisons
4ii.src: Ch 5 Poverty and inequality, slides 18-29; Ch 2 Comparative development, slides 3-6; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., p 134
4ii.watch:
• The question prints 23 1/3 marks for any three of four notes, so each note carries 7.78 marks; split them about equally between FGT and PPP.
  • P_2 satisfies all four desirable properties (anonymity, population independence, monotonicity, distributional sensitivity); the headcount ratio fails monotonicity and distributional sensitivity.
  • PPP is not the market exchange rate: market rates suit trade and debt comparisons, PPP suits living-standard comparisons.

4iii.html:
The Lewis theory (1954) is a two-sector model in which surplus labour moves from traditional agriculture to a modern industrial sector, whose growth absorbs it.

  • Traditional sector: surplus labour, with a marginal product of labour of zero, so workers can leave without loss of output; rural income W_A is the average product.
  • Modern sector: pays a fixed wage W_M above W_A, at which rural labour is in unlimited supply (a horizontal supply curve); employment is set where the marginal product of labour equals W_M.
  • Growth: capitalists reinvest all profits, so capital rises, labour demand shifts out and employment grows at a constant wage, until the surplus is absorbed (the Lewis turning point). The economy shifts from agriculture to industry.
  • Criticisms: labour-saving investment may add output but not jobs; rural surplus labour is rare, urban unemployment common.
pts: Defines the theory: surplus labour transferred from traditional agriculture to a growing modern industrial sector
Surplus labour with zero marginal product; rural income equals the average product
Fixed urban wage above rural income with unlimited (horizontal) labour supply
Profits reinvested: capital rises, labour demand shifts out, employment grows until the turning point
Gives at least two criticisms (labour-saving capital, no rural surplus or urban unemployment, rising urban wages)
4iii.src: Ch 3 Classic theories, slides 22-27; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 163-168
4iii.watch:
• Marks: Q4 prints 23 1/3 for any three of four notes, so each note is worth about 7.78; the points total 8.
  • A short note still needs the mechanism (reinvested profits shifting labour demand), not only the definition.

4iv.html:
Strategic planning for regional economic development is a long-term, participatory process by which a region (district, division or corridor) sets a vision and chooses the few strategies that best use its strengths to raise income and jobs.

Steps

  1. Organise: a lead agency with local government, business, NGOs and community groups.
  2. Situation analysis: a regional profile (population, jobs, infrastructure, resources) and a SWOT analysis to find comparative advantages.
  3. Vision and goals: measurable targets, such as jobs created by a given year.
  4. Strategies and projects: priority sectors and supporting projects (roads, power, skills, economic zones), screened by cost-benefit analysis.
  5. Action plan: who does what, when, at what cost, with what finance.
  6. Implementation: through public-private partnership and coordinated agencies.
  7. Monitoring and evaluation: track indicators, review and revise (a feedback loop).

Example: after the Padma Bridge (2022), a south-west plan could build on its port, farm and fish base with economic zones and cold chains.
pts: Defines strategic planning for regional development: a long-term, participatory process to set a vision and priorities for a region
Organising: lead agency and stakeholder participation
Situation analysis: regional profile and SWOT, identifying comparative advantages
Vision and measurable goals
Strategies: priority sectors and projects, screened by appraisal
Action plan and implementation (responsibilities, timing, finance, partnership)
Monitoring and evaluation with feedback and revision
4iv.src: Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 599-603; Standard textbook treatment
4iv.watch:
• The slides do not cover this note; the steps follow the standard strategic-planning cycle (and Todaro's sequence: set objectives, set targets, implement and monitor). Any sound sequence of five to seven steps earns the credit.
  • A plan without monitoring and revision is not strategic: always end with the feedback loop.
  • The example is illustrative; any real or hypothetical region earns the credit.

5a.html:
The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are 17 goals with 169 targets, adopted by the UN in September 2015 to be achieved by 2030, as the successor of the eight MDGs. They follow three principles: universality (every country), integration (all goals together) and transformation (no piecemeal steps).

The goals

People

  • 1 End poverty in all its forms everywhere.
  • 2 End hunger, achieve food security and nutrition, promote sustainable agriculture.
  • 3 Healthy lives and well-being for all at all ages.
  • 4 Inclusive, equitable quality education and lifelong learning.
  • 5 Gender equality and empowerment of all women and girls.

Prosperity

  • 7 Affordable, reliable, sustainable modern energy for all.
  • 8 Sustained, inclusive growth, full employment and decent work.
  • 9 Resilient infrastructure, inclusive industrialisation and innovation.
  • 10 Reduced inequality within and among countries.
  • 11 Inclusive, safe, resilient and sustainable cities.

Planet

  • 6 Water and sanitation for all.
  • 12 Sustainable consumption and production.
  • 13 Urgent action on climate change.
  • 14 Conservation of oceans and marine resources.
  • 15 Protection of land ecosystems, forests and biodiversity.

Peace and partnership

  • 16 Peaceful, inclusive societies, justice and accountable institutions.
  • 17 Means of implementation and a revitalised global partnership.
pts: Defines the SDGs: 17 goals and 169 targets, UN 2015, deadline 2030, successor of the MDGs
States the principles: universality, integration and transformation
Describes the people goals 1 to 5 (poverty, hunger, health, education, gender)
Describes the prosperity goals 7 to 11 (energy, decent work, infrastructure, inequality, cities)
Describes the planet goals 6 and 12 to 15 (water, consumption, climate, oceans, land)
Describes goals 16 and 17 (peace and institutions, partnership)
5a.src: Ch 1 Economic development (Todaro), slides 27-33; Dimensions of economic development (v3), slides 26-28
5a.watch:
• "Describe the various goals" needs each goal with a line of content, not just its number. Grouping them makes 17 items easy to recall in the exam.
  • The goal numbers are the official ones; in this grouping goal 6 (water) sits under Planet.

  • The slides' MDG criticisms (no climate goal, nothing on rights or inequality, did not apply to rich countries) are exactly what the SDGs added.

5c.html:
Achievements in the MDG era (1990-2015)

  • MDG 1: poverty fell from about 57% (1991-92) to about 24% by 2015-16, beating the halving target of 29%.
  • MDG 2 and 3: primary enrolment became nearly universal, with gender parity in primary and secondary schools.
  • MDG 4: under-5 mortality fell by about two-thirds, from about 146 per 1,000 (1990) to 46 (2014), meeting the target of 48.
  • MDG 5 and 6: maternal mortality fell steeply but missed the three-quarters cut; HIV stayed very low.
  • Shortfalls: education quality, decent jobs, environment (MDG 7).

Key challenges for the SDGs

  1. Finance: about USD 132.6 billion a year extra needed; tax revenue below 8% of GDP.
  2. Governance: weak institutions (SDG 16 declining) and slow local delivery.
  3. Leaving no one behind: widening inequality; remote regions, disabled people, urban poor.
  4. Climate and urban stress: floods, cyclones, salinity, slums and pollution.
  5. Data gaps: regular data for only about 66 of 232 indicators.
  6. LDC graduation: loss of trade preferences and cheap aid.
pts: MDG 1 achievement: poverty about halved (about 57% to about 24%), target met
Education and gender: near-universal primary enrolment and gender parity in schools
Health: under-5 mortality cut by about two-thirds; maternal mortality down (target missed)
Challenge: SDG financing gap (USD 132.6 billion a year) and low tax-to-GDP
Challenge: governance and institutional capacity, coordination or localisation
Challenge: inequality and leaving no one behind
Challenge: climate vulnerability, urbanisation, data gaps or LDC graduation

5c.watch:
• Give numbers for the MDG achievements; "Bangladesh did well" earns little. Figures from the national MDG report (2015) and Todaro's case study differ slightly in base year; give approximate values.
  • The SDG figures (financing gap, data gaps) are from the 2025 SDG deck; any well-argued challenge is creditable.

6a.html:
Given: the Harrod-Domar model links the growth rate of GDP to the national saving rate and the capital-output ratio. Assumptions: saving is a fixed share of income; output is proportional to the capital stock (a fixed capital-output ratio, labour abundant); and planned saving equals investment (closed economy, no government).

Find: the growth rate of GDP, \Delta Y / Y.

Solution. Let Y be national income, S net saving, s the net saving ratio (saving as a share of income), I net investment, K the capital stock and c the capital-output ratio (capital needed per unit of annual output).

Step 1. Saving is a fixed share of income: S = sY (3.1).

Step 2. Net investment adds to the capital stock: I = \Delta K (3.2).

Step 3. Capital is tied to output by the capital-output ratio, K/Y = c, so \Delta K/\Delta Y = c and

\Delta K = c\,\Delta Y \qquad (3.3)

Step 4. Saving equals investment, S = I (3.4). Substituting Steps 1 to 3:

S = sY = c\,\Delta Y = \Delta K = I \qquad (3.5) \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad sY = c\,\Delta Y \qquad (3.6)

Step 5. Divide both sides by Y, then by c:

\boxed{g = \frac{\Delta Y}{Y} = \frac{s}{c}} \qquad (3.7)

Answer: the growth rate of GDP equals the net saving ratio divided by the capital-output ratio. It rises with saving and falls with c; 1/c measures the productivity of investment. With s = 15\% and c = 3, g = 5\% a year. In gross terms, with depreciation rate \delta, the same steps give g = s^G/c - \delta.
pts: States the assumptions and defines s (net saving ratio) and c (capital-output ratio)
Saving function S = sY
Net investment as the change in capital, I = \Delta K
Capital-output relation K = cY, so \Delta K = c\,\Delta Y
Equates saving and investment to get sY = c\,\Delta Y
Divides by Y and c to reach \Delta Y/Y = s/c
Interprets the result: growth rises with the saving ratio and falls with the capital-output ratio (1/c is capital productivity)
6a.src: Ch 3 Classic theories, slides 8-12, 17-18; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 159-162
6a.watch:
• Use the net saving ratio with g = s/c; with gross saving, subtract the depreciation rate (g = s^G/c - \delta). Mixing them overstates growth.
  • Older texts write the capital-output ratio as k; the slides use c. Either is fine if defined.
  • The example (s = 15\%, c = 3, g = 5\%) is Todaro's equation 3.9; the question asks only for the derivation, so keep any example to one line.

6b.html:
Balanced growth (Nurkse, Rosenstein-Rodan) is simultaneous investment in many complementary industries, and in agriculture and industry together, so that sectors provide markets for each other.

Reason: in a poor country the market is too small for one factory to pay. If many expand together, each one's workers buy the others' output, breaking the vicious circle of low income, small market and low investment. It is one way to deliver the big push.
pts: Defines balanced growth: simultaneous, coordinated investment in many complementary sectors that provide markets for each other
Reason: small market and low income in poor countries (Nurkse's vicious circle); one industry alone is unprofitable
Names Nurkse or Rosenstein-Rodan, or links it to the big push or to balance between agriculture and industry
6b.src: Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 215-216, 687; Standard textbook treatment
6b.watch:
• Todaro covers the idea under the big push and coordination failure, not under the name "balanced growth"; the definition here is the standard one.
  • Its critics (Hirschman, Singer) say a poor country lacks the capital and skills to invest everywhere at once; that is part (c).

6c.html:
Unbalanced growth (Hirschman, 1958) deliberately concentrates investment in a few key sectors, so that the resulting shortages and surpluses push the rest of the economy to follow.

How it works

  • Linkages: pick industries with strong backward linkages (demand for inputs) and forward linkages (cheaper inputs for users); their growth induces investment in linked industries.
  • Induced decisions: decision-making ability is the scarcest resource; each imbalance makes the next investment obvious (a "chain of disequilibria").
  • Two paths: social overhead capital (power, roads) built ahead of demand invites private investment, or private investment runs ahead and forces public investment.

Bangladesh

  • Capital, foreign exchange and managers are too scarce to invest everywhere at once.
  • Garments: backward linkages (spinning, dyeing, accessories) and forward ones (ports, banking) grew around them.
  • Megaprojects (Padma Bridge, power plants, economic zones) are built ahead of demand to induce private investment.

Limits

  • Bottlenecks can persist: gas and power shortages hold back industry.
  • Over-dependence: garments earn over 80% of exports.
  • Agriculture and lagging regions fall behind, widening inequality.
  • Linkages leak abroad when fabric and machinery are imported.

Conclusion: unbalanced growth suits Bangladesh if key sectors are chosen for their linkages and planning corrects the imbalances; some coordinated investment (power, skills, agriculture) is still needed, so the two strategies are complements.
pts: Defines unbalanced growth (Hirschman): deliberate concentration of investment in key sectors so imbalances induce further investment
Explains backward and forward linkages and choosing sectors with the strongest linkages
Induced decision-making or the two paths (social overhead capital ahead of, or behind, directly productive activity)
Why it suits an LDC: scarce capital, foreign exchange and entrepreneurs rule out investing everywhere at once
Bangladesh application, for example RMG as a leading sector with its linkages, or megaprojects built ahead of demand
Limits: persistent bottlenecks, over-dependence on one sector, regional or sectoral inequality, or linkages leaking abroad
Credits the balanced-growth or big-push view as a sound alternative or complement
Reasoned conclusion on its suitability for Bangladesh
6c.src: Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 225-226, 687; Standard textbook treatment
6c.watch:
• "Discuss" needs both sides and a conclusion; a description of Hirschman alone earns about half.
  • The RMG share of exports varies by year and source (roughly 80 to 85% recently); say "over 80%".
  • Balanced and unbalanced growth are often presented as rivals, but both aim to overcome the small-market and coordination problems of a poor economy; a student who argues for a mix earns full credit if reasoned.

7a.html:
Development is a multidimensional process by which a society moves from a condition of life seen as unsatisfactory to one that is materially and spiritually better. It involves faster growth, less inequality and the eradication of poverty, together with changes in social structures, attitudes and institutions.

  • Beyond income: growth of GNI per capita is needed but not enough; poverty, unemployment and inequality must fall (Seers).
  • Capabilities: Sen sees development as expanding the freedom to be and do what people value (live long, be healthy, literate).
  • Objectives: more life-sustaining goods, higher levels of living and a wider range of economic and social choices.
pts: Defines development as a multidimensional process (growth, less inequality and poverty, change in structures, attitudes and institutions)
Explains that income growth is not enough: poverty, unemployment and inequality must fall
Sen's capabilities: development as expanding freedoms (beings and doings)
States the three objectives of development (or the core values sustenance, self-esteem, freedom)
7a.src: Ch 1 Economic development (Todaro), slides 16-23; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 10-13
7a.watch: • A one-line "development means economic growth" earns little; the course stresses that development is wider than growth.

7b.html:
Rostow's stages-of-growth model (1960) holds that every country passes through five sequential stages on the way to development. Bangladesh can be read against them:

  1. Traditional society: subsistence farming, limited technology. Bangladesh in the 1970s: a war-damaged rice economy with very low saving.
  2. Preconditions for take-off: farm surplus, infrastructure, education, entrepreneurs. The 1980s and 1990s: high-yield rice and irrigation, microcredit, rural roads, primary schooling and the first export garment factories.
  3. Take-off: a sharp rise in investment and leading industries. Investment rose to about 30% of GDP by the late 2010s and growth to 6 to 8%, with garments the leading sector.
  4. Drive to maturity: diversification and fewer imports. Not yet reached: garments are 84% of exports and machinery is imported; pharmaceuticals and ICT are early signs.
  5. High mass consumption: durable goods and services. Far off, though an urban middle class is growing.

Assessment: Bangladesh is in or near take-off. The fit is loose: services already exceed half of GDP, growth rests on low-wage exports and remittances, and saving alone has not sufficed, with private investment stuck near 23% of GDP and weak institutions.
pts: Defines the model: all countries pass through sequential stages to development
Traditional society: features, and Bangladesh's early subsistence economy
Preconditions: features, and Bangladesh's high-yield rice and irrigation, microcredit, schooling, roads or the first garment factories
Take-off: rising investment and leading sectors, with Bangladesh evidence (investment about 30% of GDP, garments, faster growth)
Drive to maturity: features, and why Bangladesh has not reached it (narrow exports, import dependence)
High mass consumption: features, and its distance for Bangladesh
Places Bangladesh at a stage with reasons (take-off, or another placement that is argued)
A limit of the model for Bangladesh (overlapping stages, services-led growth, saving not sufficient, weak institutions)
7b.src: Ch 3 Classic theories, slides 3-7, 19-21; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 159, 162-163; Bangladesh and the SDGs (2026), slide 6
7b.watch:
• There is no official "stage" for Bangladesh; placing it in the preconditions stage, or early in the drive to maturity, is acceptable if argued with evidence.
  • The figures are approximate national-accounts values (investment about 30% of GDP, services over half of GDP); the 84% export share and private investment near 23% of GDP are from the course's SDG deck.
  • The paper is from 2016-17; growth slowed after 2020, which strengthens the "saving is not sufficient" point.

7c.html:
(i) Dynamic entrepreneurship

An entrepreneur organises land, labour and capital, bears risk and introduces new ideas. Schumpeter's dynamic entrepreneur is an innovator: new products, methods, markets, supply sources or organisation. Better firms displace old ones ("creative destruction"), driving growth. Entrepreneurs turn saving into investment, adopt technology and create jobs and exports, as Bangladesh's garment entrepreneurs have since 1978. They need credit, secure property rights and little red tape.

(ii) Technological progress

Technological progress means new and improved ways of doing traditional tasks. Its forms (slide 36):

  • neutral: more output from the same inputs;
  • labour-saving or capital-saving (the latter suits labour-abundant countries);
  • labour-augmenting (training) or capital-augmenting (steel instead of wooden ploughs).

It shifts the production possibility frontier outward; in the Solow model it is the only source of sustained growth in income per head. High-yield rice (IR-8 and later varieties) doubled or tripled yields in parts of Asia.
pts: (i) Defines the entrepreneur: organises factors, bears risk, innovates
(i) Schumpeter's innovator (new products, methods, markets, sources or organisation) and creative destruction
(i) Role in growth (turns saving into investment, jobs, exports), with an example or the conditions it needs
(ii) Defines technological progress: new ways of accomplishing tasks
(ii) Types: neutral, labour- or capital-saving, labour- or capital-augmenting
(ii) Effect on growth (PPF shifts outward; sustained growth per head), with an example such as high-yield rice
7c.src: Ch 3 Classic theories, slides 36-40; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 188, 190-193; Standard textbook treatment
7c.watch:
• Entrepreneurship is not on the chapter 3 slides; the Schumpeter account is the standard textbook treatment.
  • Each part carries about half the marks; do not write a long (i) and a one-line (ii).
  • Capital-saving progress is the type labour-rich countries need most, yet most research produces labour-saving technology.

8a.html:
Investment in economics is spending on new real capital (machinery, buildings, roads, power plants, inventories, and skills as human capital) that adds to the economy's productive capacity. It means giving up present consumption for a stream of future returns. Buying existing shares or land is financial investment: it transfers ownership but adds no new capital. Net investment is gross investment minus depreciation.

Basis of the decision. Money has a time value, so an investment is worth making only if its expected returns, discounted at the cost of funds, exceed its cost. In Keynes's terms, invest while the marginal efficiency of capital exceeds the rate of interest.

Criteria

  1. Payback period: years to recover the outlay; shorter is safer. A liquidity and risk screen, but it ignores later returns.
  2. Accounting rate of return: average profit divided by average investment, compared with a target.
  3. Net present value: \mathrm{NPV} = \sum CF_t/(1+r)^t; invest if positive. The most reliable criterion, measuring the value added.
  4. Internal rate of return: the rate at which NPV = 0 (the marginal efficiency of capital); invest if above the cost of capital.
  5. Benefit-cost ratio or profitability index: PV(B)/PV(C) above 1; ranks projects when capital is rationed.
  6. Risk: sensitivity tests on costs, benefits and the discount rate, or a risk premium in r.
  7. Social criteria for public or development investment: shadow prices for labour and foreign exchange, employment created, income distribution and environmental effects.

Rule: accept projects with positive NPV, rank by NPV (or by BCR under a budget limit), and use the others as checks.
pts: Defines investment as an addition to real capital (plant, machinery, infrastructure, inventories), giving up present consumption for future returns
Distinguishes real from financial investment, or gross from net investment
Basis: discounted returns compared with the cost of funds (marginal efficiency of capital against the interest rate)
Payback criterion with its use and limitation
Accounting rate of return
NPV criterion: formula, invest if positive, why it is the most reliable
IRR criterion: rate giving NPV = 0, invest if above the cost of capital
BCR or profitability index above 1; ranking under capital rationing
Risk and social criteria (sensitivity, shadow prices, employment, distribution, environment), or the development-economics criteria such as social marginal productivity or the reinvestment criterion
8a.src: CBA exam note, pp 5-9; Solved problems: NPV, IRR, payback, pp 1-4; Cost-benefit analysis handout, handout parts III-VIII and XI; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 608-610; Standard textbook treatment
8a.watch:
• The question is open: a development-economics answer (capital-turnover criterion, social marginal productivity, the Galenson-Leibenstein reinvestment criterion, Sen's time-series criterion) is also creditable for the criteria marks, as long as each is explained.
  • Do not define investment as "buying shares": in economics that is a financial transfer, not investment.
  • The IRR is the project-level counterpart of Keynes's marginal efficiency of capital.

8b.html:
The slides group the classic theories of development into four approaches:

  1. Linear stages of growth. Development is a sequence of stages (Rostow: traditional society to high mass consumption), driven by saving and investment. Harrod-Domar gives g = s/c: growth rises with the saving rate s and falls with the capital-output ratio c. Limit: capital is necessary but not sufficient.
  2. Structural change. An agrarian economy becomes an industrial one. In the Lewis two-sector model, surplus farm labour moves to a modern sector that reinvests its profits; Chenery's patterns of development trace the changes empirically. Limit: rural surplus labour is rare.
  3. International dependence. Underdevelopment is caused from outside: neocolonial dependence (unequal centre-periphery power, local elites), the false-paradigm model (inappropriate foreign advice) and the dualistic-development thesis (rich and poor coexist; the gap persists). Limit: it explains poverty but not how to develop.
  4. Neoclassical counter-revolution. Underdevelopment comes from price distortions and too much state intervention; the free-market, public-choice and market-friendly approaches, with the Solow growth model. Limit: markets also fail.

Conclusion: no single paradigm is accepted; each theory adds part of the picture.
pts: Linear stages: Rostow's sequence of stages and Harrod-Domar (g = s/c), with the saving-investment logic
Structural change: the Lewis two-sector model (surplus labour, reinvested profits), or Chenery's patterns
Dependence: the neocolonial, false-paradigm and dualistic strands (at least two named and explained)
Neoclassical counter-revolution: markets over state (free market, public choice, market-friendly) or the Solow model
A limitation of each, or the conclusion that no single paradigm is accepted
8b.src: Ch 3 Classic theories, slides 2-4, 8-9, 19-22, 27, 30-35; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 159-176
8b.watch:
• "Briefly discuss" with 10 1/3 marks: about three lines per theory plus a limitation; do not write a full Lewis answer.
  • Newer approaches (endogenous growth, coordination failure) are welcome extras but not needed.
  • Marks: printed as 10 1/3; the points total 10.5.
